digest.top_line: Electron RT for BCC/SCC: 3-yr LRF 97.5% (54 Gy/18fx) vs 96.1% (44 Gy/10fx), no difference in either histology; retrospective, dose assigned by frailty.
digest.tldr: Skin RT carried the day: retrospective NMSC cohorts support hypofractionation, with 44 Gy/10fx matching 54 Gy/18fx and ≤2 Gy/fx predicting BCC failure (p=0.01), while a UK survey found 24 different non-standard regimens. In CNS, a GK-vs-VMAT replanning study puts the Linac SRS crossover near 0.4 cc, on dosimetric surrogates only.

sites.intro: Four NMSC RT reports, all retrospective or survey-based: fraction size and lesion size recur as the levers for local control, and real-world schedules vary widely.

studies.name: UK practice survey of NMSC radiotherapy
studies.tldr: Of 63 UK respondents, most chose one of four daily schedules (18-20 Gy/1#, 35 Gy/5#, 45 Gy/10#, 55 Gy/20#). Non-standard schedules varied widely, with 24 different regimens proposed.
details: 🔍 Anonymous online scenario-based survey of UK clinical oncologists; 43 complete, 20 partial responses
🔍 Each scenario posed for a healthy 65yo, a relatively well 80yo, and an 85yo nursing home resident with early dementia
🔍 kV access in 81% of responders; 46.2% treat <5 skin cases per month

details.text: 📊 Popularity of commonly suggested dose fractionations (Table 1)

💊 Fitness drove the schedule: longer courses for fitter pts, single fraction or non-standard for the infirm elderly

⚠️ Authors state 22 Gy single fraction should no longer be acceptable unless correcting for stand-off
⚠️ Hypothetical scenario stems, no clinic gestalt; only 43 completed surveys

verdict.rationale: Scenario-based practice-pattern survey with no outcome endpoint; it reports clinician preference, and the authors' fractionation recommendations rest on retrospective series and BED modelling.
verdict.audience: NMSC (BCC/SCC) for primary RT, across fitness strata

studies.significance: The actionable signal is the non-standard (less-than-daily) schedules for frail pts: 24 different regimens were proposed, and the authors' BED modelling flags 28 Gy/2# 6 weeks apart, 32.4 Gy/3# weekly and 36 Gy/4# weekly as carrying too much late-effect risk. The authors also say a 22 Gy single fraction should be dropped unless it corrects for stand-off.
studies.monday_clinic: For a frail elderly pt with NMSC who cannot manage daily visits, this questions the weekly 28 Gy/2#, 32.4 Gy/3# and 36 Gy/4# schedules on late-effect grounds. It does not inform the fit pt, where daily 35 Gy/5# to 55 Gy/20# matched the published series.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Anonymous online survey sent through the clinical heads of service and audit leads at **58** UK centres, open for 3 months. **43 complete and 20 partial** responses.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: UK clinical oncologists treating NMSC. Each scenario assumed tissue diagnosis and an MDT decision for **primary RT**, posed for a healthy 65yo, a relatively well 80yo, and an 85yo nursing home resident with early dementia.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Responses grouped as single fractions, 3-5 fx (27.5-35.0 Gy), 8-10 fx (32-45 Gy), 15-33 fx (45-66 Gy), non-standard alternate-day / twice-weekly / weekly, brachytherapy, and palliative. **kV available to 81%**. Electrons were favoured for larger lesions and younger pts.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Four schedules dominated: **18-20 Gy/1#, 35 Gy/5#, 45 Gy/10#, 55 Gy/20#**. Non-standard practice was heterogeneous, with **24 different** fractionations. kV use split by site: **>80%** for a 1.5-cm ala nasi BCC vs **around 25%** for a 2-cm helical SCC.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: No prospective trials exist to compare against. The authors judge daily schedules consistent with retrospective hypofractionation series (44-45 Gy/10# or 35 Gy/5#), and single-fraction dosing consistent with data favouring 18 or 20 Gy over 22 Gy for cosmesis and necrosis.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents UK clinical oncologist preference for primary RT of BCC/SCC across fitness strata. Does not represent outcomes, adjuvant RT after excision, or high-risk nodal disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Responses are stated preference for hypothetical stems, not audited delivered treatment. The BED comparison depends on assumed parameters (α/β 8.5 Gy tumour, 3 Gy late, Tk 28 days), and no fitness-stratified outcome data were collected.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Daily practice is broadly harmonized. The real gap is the frail-elderly non-standard regimens and graft recurrence volumes, where an almost even split between whole-graft and recurrence-plus-margin reflects missing data rather than a considered choice.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this survey is not that it shows UK skin RT is well aligned with the evidence. There is very little evidence to align with, and the authors themselves describe the published base as retrospective series and case reviews. What the survey does is mark where consensus has formed without trial data and where it has not. Daily schedules converge on a small set (35 Gy/5#, 45 Gy/10#, 55 Gy/20#, and 18-20 Gy single fraction), and those match the retrospective series the authors cite. This convergence is best read as inherited institutional practice that happens to agree with retrospective data, not as validation of any one schedule against another.

The heterogeneity that matters is in the frailest pts, where 24 different less-than-daily regimens were proposed. This is the clinical setting where follow-up is weakest: the authors acknowledge these pts are often not reviewed regularly after treatment, so local failures and late toxicity are under-ascertained. The authors' linear-quadratic comparison is the most useful analytic piece. It suggests the three most popular non-standard schedules are radiobiologically similar, and that 28 Gy/2# 6 weeks apart, 32.4 Gy/3# weekly and 36 Gy/4# weekly may carry excess late-effect risk. A reader should hold this loosely. The tumour α/β of 8.5 Gy, the kick-off time and the repopulation terms are borrowed estimates, and a time-correction term built on a 4-day doubling time is a model assumption, not a skin-cancer measurement. The direction of the warning is plausible. The ranking among the safer schedules is not well supported by this calculation.

The site-specific findings show clinicians weighing anatomy against what the literature says. Over 80% chose kV for a small ala nasi BCC, but only around 25% did so for a helical SCC, even though the cited retrospective data report good control and low late morbidity with kV at the ear. The authors offer vascular tolerance as a possible reason. A simpler one is that a single bad chondronecrosis case shapes an individual clinician's practice more than any series does. The refusal rates for the shin (around 20%) and the 7.7% who declined to treat the hand, despite the scenario stating the pt was unfit for surgery, show the same conservatism. In both cases brachytherapy, which the authors note has favourable data for the hand, was rarely chosen.

Methodologically, this is stated preference for hypothetical cases from 43 complete respondents, many of whom treat fewer than 5 skin cases a month, and it dates from 2014. It cannot show that any schedule controls disease better. Its lasting use is narrower: it supports dropping 22 Gy single fractions without stand-off correction, it gives grounds to question the most hypofractionated weekly regimens in pts who may live long enough to see late effects, and it identifies graft recurrence volumes and frail-elderly fractionation as the places where pooled local outcome data would change practice soonest.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The actionable signal is the non-standard (less-than-daily) schedules for frail pts: 24 different regimens were proposed, and the authors' BED modelling flags 28 Gy/2# 6 weeks apart, 32.4 Gy/3# weekly and 36 Gy/4# weekly as carrying too much late-effect risk. The authors also say a 22 Gy single fraction should be dropped unless it corrects for stand-off.

open_questions: Which non-standard fractionation is safest and most effective in frail elderly NMSC?
Whole graft vs recurrence-plus-margin volume for in-graft recurrence
Does kV over ear cartilage carry excess late toxicity?

studies.name: Radiotherapy for epithelial skin cancer (Locke)
studies.tldr: Local control 89% overall (93% untreated vs 80% recurrent) across 531 BCC/SCC lesions; dose/fx <2 Gy predicted local failure (p=0.01).
details: 🔍 Single-institution retrospective review, 468 pts / 531 lesions treated 1966-1997
🔍 389 BCC, 142 SCC; 167 lesions recurrent after prior surgery, electrodessication or outside RT
🔍 Median f/u 5.8 yr (range 2-24); minimum 2 yr unless death or lost to f/u
💊 Modality: superficial x-rays 60%, electrons 19%, electrons + superficial 20%, megavoltage photons <2%
🔍 Treatment volume: tumor plus microscopic extension, additional margin of 1 cm depending on size

details.text: 📊 Local control by histology and presentation
📊 BCC 1.1-5 cm: local control by dose per fraction (Table 5)

details: 📐 ≤2 Gy vs larger fx sizes for BCC 1.1-5 cm: p=0.01
⚠️ SCC showed no clear dose response and no significant fx-size difference (p=0.13 for lesions ≤1 cm)

subdetails: Daily fx size: larger fx = better control, p=0.01
Maximal lesion diameter and histology (SCC vs BCC): p<0.01
Modality (electrons vs other): p=0.345, not significant
Age p=0.164; number of treatment days p=0.144

details: 📊 Crude LC by modality: superficial 94% (299 of 317), electrons 82% (82 of 100), combination 82% (89 of 108)
📊 T4 SCC: cartilage invasion 75% (9 of 12), bony invasion 67% (14 of 21)
📊 SCC nodal involvement 14% (11/79) untreated vs 32% (20/62) recurrent

subdetails: 92% excellent/good among pts with cosmesis data
Fair/poor: superficial 12 (4%) of 276, electrons 10 (12%) of 81, combination 15 (19%) of 77
Overall complications 5.8% (13% in lesions >5 cm)
Soft-tissue necrosis: SCC 13 (9%) of 142, BCC 8 (2%) of 389

details: ⚠️ Modality not randomized: electrons used for larger lesions, so crude modality differences are confounded by size
⚠️ Cosmesis graded retrospectively from records and photos; data missing for 15-25% of untreated lesions
🔗 vs Lovett et al. (same institution, 1986): electrons were worse on multivariate there; authors attribute the loss of significance to larger electron margins in later years
🔗 Consistent with Silva et al. (pinna lesions): <2 Gy/fx was a significant factor for recurrence on multivariate analysis

verdict.rationale: Retrospective single-institution series spanning three decades; modality chosen by lesion size, not randomized, so dose and modality associations are confounded. No surgical comparator.
verdict.audience: Cutaneous BCC/SCC, untreated or recurrent, definitive RT

studies.significance: The dose-per-fraction signal is confined to BCC 1.1-5 cm: 75% LC at ≤2 Gy/fx vs 95-100% at larger fx sizes (p=0.01), with no equivalent effect for SCC. Recurrent SCC is the weak group (68% LC, 32% nodal involvement), which bears on whether a recurrent SCC field should be treated more aggressively than a primary.
studies.monday_clinic: In a 1-5 cm BCC planned for definitive RT, this series argues against conventional ≤2 Gy fractions; it says nothing about fraction size for SCC, where no dose response was seen.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-institution **retrospective** review of consecutive pts treated **1966-1997**. 468 pts, 531 lesions; median f/u **5.8 yr** (range 2-24).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Biopsy-proven epithelial skin cancer: **389 BCC, 142 SCC**; 364 previously untreated, **167 recurrent**. Median age 73 (BCC) and 72 (SCC).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Superficial x-rays 60%, electrons 19%, electrons + superficial 20%, megavoltage photons <2%. Volume was tumor plus microscopic extension, with an **additional 1 cm margin** depending on size; lead eye shields when near the eye, and bolus use evolved over time.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Local control (relapse-free from RT start), cosmesis (telangiectasia, pigment change, fibrosis) and complications.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Overall LC **89%**; untreated 93% vs recurrent 80%. On multivariate analysis, **fraction size (p=0.01)**, lesion diameter and histology (p<0.01) predicted local failure; **modality did not (p=0.345)**.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Complications **5.8%** overall (13% for lesions >5 cm), mainly soft-tissue necrosis: 9% of SCC vs 2% of BCC. Fair/poor cosmesis was 4% with superficial RT vs 12% electrons and 19% combination.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The same institution's 1986 series (Lovett et al.) found electrons worse on multivariate analysis. Here that association disappears, which the authors attribute to wider electron margins in later years. The <2 Gy/fx failure signal matches Silva et al. in pinna lesions.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents cutaneous BCC and SCC treated with definitive superficial or electron RT, including recurrent lesions. Does not represent modern image-guided or brachytherapy techniques, or nodal management of high-risk cutaneous SCC.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Treatment spans three decades with evolving bolus and margin policy. The cosmesis data are missing for 15-25% of untreated lesions, and the SCC dose cells are small, so the absent SCC dose response may reflect low power.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The data support RT as definitive therapy for early BCC/SCC and put the main lever on **fraction size and lesion size**, not beam type. Recurrent SCC carries the poorest control and the most cosmetic cost, so failure at first treatment is expensive.

studies.interpretation:
The most useful read of this series is the fractionation finding, and it is narrower than the headline suggests. For BCC 1.1 to 5 cm, local control was 75% at 2 Gy or less per fraction against 95 to 100% at larger fraction sizes, and fraction size survived multivariate analysis (p=0.01). That fits the long clinical habit of hypofractionating cutaneous BCC and the result reported by Silva et al. for pinna lesions. But the effect sits in one histology and one size band. For SCC the authors found no clear dose response and no significant fraction-size difference, and the per-cell counts are small enough that this should be read as absence of evidence, not evidence of absence. A reader should not extend the BCC fractionation argument to SCC on the strength of this paper.

The modality comparison needs more caution than the crude numbers invite. Superficial x-rays controlled 94% of lesions against 82% for electrons and for combination treatment, which looks like a clear gradient until you remember how beams were assigned. Electrons went to larger and deeper lesions, and size was itself an independent predictor of failure. Once diameter, histology and fraction size were in the model, modality fell away (p=0.345). The authors make an interesting internal comparison: their own 1986 series had found electrons worse on multivariate analysis, and they attribute the change to wider electron margins in later years. That is plausible and clinically relevant, since electron penumbra at the skin surface is the classic way to underdose a lateral edge, but it is an explanation offered after the fact rather than something the design can test. The margin tables point the same way for SCC with 1 cm or smaller electron margins, without reaching significance.

The recurrent-disease data carry the most practical weight. Recurrent SCC had 68% local control and 32% nodal involvement, compared with 89% and 14% for untreated SCC, and recurrent SCC also had the worst cosmesis. One third of the cohort had already failed a prior treatment, so this is not a rare scenario. The finding argues that the first treatment of a cutaneous SCC is where control is won or lost, whatever modality is used, and that a recurrent lesion should be staged and managed as higher-risk disease, nodal basin included.

The main reasons for caution are structural. The series spans 1966 to 1997, with bolus and margin policy changing along the way. Cosmesis was graded retrospectively from notes and photographs and is missing for a meaningful fraction of lesions. There is no surgical or Mohs comparator, so the paper says nothing about whether RT should be chosen over excision. What it can support is that, when RT is chosen, lesion size, histology and fraction size drive control far more than beam choice.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: For BCC 1.1-5 cm, ≤2 Gy/fx gave 75% LC vs 95-100% with larger fractions (p=0.01), with no such effect in SCC. Modality dropped out on multivariate analysis (p=0.345) once electron margins widened, so margin and fraction size matter more than beam choice.

open_questions: Optimal hypofractionation schedule for cutaneous SCC
Elective nodal coverage for recurrent cutaneous SCC
Do modern electron margins and bolus close the gap with superficial RT?

studies.name: Hypofractionated electron beam RT for epithelial skin cancer, 434 cases
studies.tldr: 3-yr actuarial LRF 97.5% (54 Gy/18fx) vs 96.1% (44 Gy/10fx) with electrons for BCC/SCC; no significant difference in either histology.
details: 🔍 Single-centre retrospective series: 434 biopsy-proven tumours in 333 pts, treated 2001-2006
🔍 332 BCC (76.5%), 102 SCC (23.5%); 386 primary RT after biopsy, 48 postop for residual disease

subdetails: 54 Gy in 18 fx of 3 Gy (n=159) vs 44 Gy in 10 fx of 4.4 Gy (n=275), four fx per week
Electron energy 4-12 MeV, chosen by estimated tumour depth
Target: tumour + 1 cm margin
Skin-sparing compensated with copper foil (0.2 mm at 4 MeV, 0.4 mm at 6-12 MeV)

details.text: 📊 3-yr actuarial local recurrence-free rate by histology and dose

details: 📊 T stage was the only factor tied to local recurrence (log-rank p=0.036)
📊 T3 (>5 cm): 2/11 recurred, one BCC and one SCC, both after 44 Gy

subdetails: Median time to LR 6.3 mo (range 1-65)
BCC: 10/332 recurred, median 10.4 mo; all local-only, all treated by complete excision
SCC: 5/102 recurred, median 3.3 mo; 3 of 5 also developed metastases

details: 📊 3-yr MFS 98.8% overall (94.7% SCC, 100% BCC); 3-yr OS 54% SCC, 82% BCC; CSS 98% and 100%

details.text: 📊 Cosmesis, pilot set of 14 pts (no significant difference between schedules)

details: ⚠️ Dose assigned by era and frailty, not randomised: elderly, less mobile pts got 44 Gy first; standard from Jan 2004
⚠️ Age imbalance: >80y in 41.2% of 44 Gy vs 17.0% of 54 Gy tumours
⚠️ Shorter follow-up in the 44 Gy group, acknowledged by the authors
⚠️ Per-tumour analysis, no correction for pts with multiple lesions; univariate only (too few events)
⚠️ BCC 44 Gy 3-yr LRF given as 96.9% in Results text but 96.7% in the Fig 1 caption
⚠️ Cosmesis from 14 pts, photographed at median 66 mo (54 Gy) vs 22 mo (44 Gy): unequal time for late effects

verdict.rationale: Single-centre retrospective; schedule assigned by era and frailty, older 44 Gy cohort with shorter follow-up; univariate only, 15 events total. Cosmesis from 14 pts.
verdict.audience: Biopsy-proven BCC or SCC, mostly head/face, elderly, primary or postop residual

studies.significance: The boundary is size: T3 tumours >5 cm recurred in 2/11, both after 44 Gy, so the centre now gives 54 Gy above 5 cm. SCC behaves differently from BCC. SCC recurrences came early (median 3.3 mo) and 3 of 5 had metastases. All BCC recurrences were local-only and treated by excision. Technique was a 1 cm margin with copper-foil compensation for skin sparing.
studies.monday_clinic: In an elderly pt with T1-T2 BCC or SCC on the face or head treated with electrons, this supports 44 Gy/10 fx as a convenience schedule equivalent in observed control to 54 Gy/18 fx; it does not extend to lesions >5 cm.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective single-centre series**, 434 tumours in 333 pts treated January 2001 to December 2006. Analysis per tumour; LRF and MFS as one minus cumulative incidence with death as competing risk.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Biopsy-proven BCC (n=332) or SCC (n=102)**, primary RT (n=386) or postop for residual disease (n=48). Median age 74.8y BCC, 78.3y SCC; 59.4% face, 22.4% elsewhere on head.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Electrons, **54 Gy/18 fx of 3 Gy (n=159) or 44 Gy/10 fx of 4.4 Gy (n=275)**, four fx per week. 4-12 MeV by tumour depth, tumour + 1 cm margin, copper foil to offset skin sparing.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: No significant LRF difference between schedules in BCC (p=0.67) or SCC (p=0.46). **T stage was the only factor associated with local recurrence (p=0.036)**; gender, age, histology, indication, site, dose and lesion number were not.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Toxicity not reported beyond cosmesis. In a 14-pt pilot, pt-scored good/fair cosmesis was 75% (54 Gy) and 100% (44 Gy), observer-scored 87% and 83%, **no significant difference**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The authors cite RT local control of 87-97% for BCC and 56-91% for SCC in prior series, placing these rates at or above that range. They describe them as comparable to surgical series.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents elderly pts with T1-T2 BCC or SCC, mostly head and face, treated with electrons and a 1 cm margin. Does not represent tumours >5 cm, where both 44 Gy T3 failures occurred.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Frail pts were moved to 44 Gy before it became standard, which may bias toward fewer recurrences being seen (competing deaths) rather than toward better control. **SCC CIs are wide** (54 Gy lower bound 79.1%), so equivalence for SCC is not shown.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The authors argue follow-up was adequate because recurrences came early (median 10.4 mo BCC, 3.3 mo SCC). They conclude 44 Gy/10 fx is optimal for T1-T2 disease. The data support non-inferior-looking control at small size, not a formal non-inferiority claim.

studies.interpretation:
This is a single-institution, era-based comparison of two electron schedules. Its value is less the head-to-head than its documentation of where a ten-fraction course stops working. Overall 3-year actuarial local recurrence-free rates of 97.5% and 96.1% sit at the upper end of the RT ranges the authors cite from prior series (87-97% for BCC, 56-91% for SCC). For BCC treated to 44 Gy, the confidence interval runs from 93.1% to 98.8%, tight enough that a reader can accept the shorter course for small lesions without much worry about giving up control.

SCC is weaker ground. Only 102 SCCs were treated, 33 of them to 54 Gy, and the 54 Gy interval reaches down to 79.1%. A log-rank p of 0.46 in that setting says the study could not see a difference, not that none exists. The pattern of SCC failure also deserves more weight than the headline. Recurrences arrived at a median of 3.3 months, and three of the five came with metastases. That is early, biologically aggressive failure, and the paper does not tie it to dose.

The allocation mechanism is the methodological problem a skeptic will press. 44 Gy was first given to elderly, less mobile pts, so 41.2% of the 44 Gy tumours were in pts over 80, against 17.0% in the 54 Gy group, and follow-up was shorter in the 44 Gy group. In a population whose 3-year OS for SCC was 54%, competing mortality can hide local failures. The competing-risk method handles this in the estimate but cannot recover events in pts who died before failing. So the bias plausibly runs in favour of the hypofractionated arm. The defence, that most recurrences in this series appeared within the first year, is reasonable for BCC and SCC as observed here. It does not settle the comparison.

The T-stage signal is the actionable part. Two of 11 tumours larger than 5 cm recurred, both after 44 Gy, and the centre responded by returning those lesions to 54 Gy. Eleven tumours cannot carry a dose-response conclusion, but they mark the edge of the evidence: the 44 Gy result is a T1-T2 result. The technique details are what make the result reproducible: a 1 cm margin, energy matched to depth, and copper-foil compensation for the electron surface dose. A centre using tighter margins or no surface compensation should not assume the same control rates.

The cosmesis data come from 14 pts photographed at very different intervals (median 66 vs 22 months). They show that the larger fraction size did not produce obviously worse appearance in this small sample, and they say nothing about very late effects of 4.4 Gy fractions. What would make this conclusion wrong is a randomised or matched comparison showing excess late failure or late fibrosis after the shorter course in SCC or larger lesions, which this design cannot exclude.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Size sets the limit: T3 >5 cm recurred in 2/11, both after 44 Gy, and the centre now uses 54 Gy above 5 cm. SCC failures came early (median 3.3 mo) and 3 of 5 had metastases. BCC failures were local-only and treated by excision. Technique was a 1 cm margin with copper-foil surface compensation.

open_questions: Is 44 Gy/10 fx adequate for SCC, given wide CIs?
Late cosmesis and fibrosis after 4.4 Gy fractions beyond 2 years

studies.name: Predictors of recurrence after RT for NMSC
studies.tldr: Recurrence 15.8% at median 18.4 mo across 448 RT-treated NMSCs; age, size ≥2 cm, immunosuppression and photon modality independently predicted recurrence.
details: 🔍 Single-centre cohort from a prospective database, Odette Cancer Centre multidisciplinary clinic, 2007-2011
🔍 389 pts, 448 lesions; median age 78; BCC 46.2%, sclerosing BCC 25.7%, SCC 28.1%
🔍 Indication: primary 53.3%, recurrent after prior tx 29.7%, postoperative 16.7%; face 63.2% of lesions
📊 Overall LC 84.2%; median time to recurrence 11.4 mo (range 6.5-23.8)

details.text: 📐 Multivariate predictors of recurrence (logistic regression, per tumour)

subdetails: Orthovoltage 41.1%, electrons 32.6%, megavoltage photons 26.3%
Most common: 50 Gy/20 fx (26.3%) and 40 Gy/10 fx (14.5%)
Margin 1-2 cm to field edge; electrons/photons for tumours >1 cm thick or >3 cm

details: 📐 No dose signal: EQD2 OR 1.007, p=0.4735 on univariate
📐 SCC vs BCC OR 1.890 on univariate; pathology dropped out after backwards selection
📐 Recurrent vs primary lesions: OR 1.597, p=0.1014, a trend only
⚠️ Photon effect likely confounding by indication: photons reserved for deeper, larger lesions (authors' own read)
⚠️ Logistic regression on a time-dependent outcome; censoring ignored with follow-up range 0-132 mo
⚠️ Per-tumour analysis, no correction for multiple lesions per pt
🔗 LC below the literature ranges cited by authors (BCC 87%-98%, SCC 56%-97%); van Hezewijk 44/10 vs 54/18 3y LC 96.1% vs 96.9%

verdict.rationale: Single-centre retrospective analysis; logistic model ignores censoring, modality effect confounded by indication, and 18.4-mo median f/u undercounts late BCC recurrence.
verdict.audience: BCC/SCC skin cancer treated with RT, primary/recurrent/postop, median age 78

studies.significance: Dose did not predict control (EQD2 OR 1.007, p=0.4735), while size ≥2 cm (OR 2.090) and immunosuppression (OR 2.939) did. Within the 40/10 and 50/20 schedules used here, escalation is not supported by this cohort; the lesion and host define risk. The photon OR is a marker of deeper, larger targets, not an argument against megavoltage.
studies.monday_clinic: In an immunosuppressed pt or a lesion ≥2 cm referred for skin RT, this supports counseling on a higher recurrence risk and closer follow-up past 2 years; it does not show that photons themselves are inferior for deep lesions.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-centre analysis of a **prospectively maintained database**, RT delivered 2007-2011. Recurrence was assessed clinically. Univariate then backwards logistic regression, **per tumour**, with no correction for multiple lesions per pt.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **389 pts, 448 BCC/SCC lesions**, median age 78 (41-99). 67.9% <2 cm; 9% in immunosuppressed pts. Primary 53.3%, recurrent 29.7%, postoperative 16.7%.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Orthovoltage 100-300 kV, electrons 6-18 MeV with bolus, or 1-2 field photons (IMRT selectively). Most common schedules **50 Gy/20 fx** and **40 Gy/10 fx**. GTV by clinical mark-up plus a **1-2 cm margin**; CT planning for deep tumours.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: LC **84.2%** at median f/u 18.4 mo; median time to recurrence 11.4 mo. Independent predictors were age, **size ≥2 cm**, **immunosuppression** and **modality**; EQD2 and indication (primary vs recurrent vs postop) were not.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: LC sits below the ranges the authors cite (BCC 87%-98%, SCC 56%-97%). The van Hezewijk series used higher-EQD2 schedules (44/10 vs 54/18) with 3y LC 96.1% and 96.9%, but the populations are not comparable.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents elderly pts with BCC/SCC of mostly face, ear and scalp treated with orthovoltage, electrons or photons to moderate hypofractionated schedules. Does not represent nodal or perineural-predominant cSCC, or long-term late recurrence beyond ~2 years.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Logistic regression treats a time-to-event outcome as binary, so pts with 0-mo follow-up count as controlled. The 3-category modality variable cannot separate technique from tumour depth. Recurrence was not split into in-field vs marginal.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The independent risk factors are patient and tumour features, not dose, which points to selection and target coverage rather than prescription as the lever. The **modality OR reflects case mix** per the authors and should not drive technique choice.

studies.interpretation:
The useful signal in this series is what did not predict recurrence. Across a cohort treated mostly with 50 Gy in 20 fractions or 40 Gy in 10, EQD2 carried no association with outcome (OR 1.007, p=0.4735), and whether a lesion was primary, recurrent, or treated postoperatively did not reach significance either. What remained after backwards selection were host and tumour features: age, size of 2 cm or greater, and immunosuppression, each with odds ratios in a range that matters clinically (2.090 for size, 2.939 for immunosuppression). For a radiation oncologist deciding on a schedule, the implication is that within the conventional hypofractionated range used here, prescription is not the lever; the lesion and the host define the risk, and the reader's effort belongs in target definition and surveillance.

The modality finding needs to be read the way the authors themselves read it. Orthovoltage and electrons outperformed photons (ORs 0.285 and 0.440), but photons were reserved by protocol for tumours thicker than 1 cm or larger than 3 cm. That is confounding by indication built into the treatment algorithm, and a three-level modality variable cannot be adjusted away by also including a dichotomized size term, because depth and true extent are not captured by the 2 cm cut. The photon OR is best treated as a marker of the deep, extensive lesion, not as evidence that megavoltage technique fails. If anything, it argues for scrutiny of margins and bolus on those cases, since inadequate field size has been raised elsewhere as an explanation for modality differences.

Several methodological choices should lower confidence in the absolute numbers. Recurrence was modeled with logistic regression rather than a time-to-event method, so a lesion followed for zero months counts as controlled alongside one followed for a decade. With a median follow-up of 18.4 months and discharge of BCC at 2 years, late recurrences, which are characteristic of BCC, are structurally undercounted, and the 84.2% control rate is both lower than many series and probably still optimistic for the longer horizon. The analysis is per tumour without correction for multiple lesions per patient, which matters most for the immunosuppressed group, where one transplant recipient can contribute several correlated events. Recurrence was a clinical judgment without a stated in-field versus marginal distinction, so pattern-of-failure inference is not possible.

Against the van Hezewijk comparison the authors raise, where higher-EQD2 schedules reported 3-year control around 96%, the temptation is to attribute the gap to dose. This dataset does not support that reading, both because its own dose variable was null and because the populations differ in recurrent and postoperative case mix. The age association is also worth holding loosely: the authors note most prior work finds no age effect, and a small per-year OR in an elderly cohort can reflect competing follow-up patterns as easily as biology.

What would make the main conclusions wrong is a clustering or censoring artefact concentrated in the high-risk groups. A competing-risk or Cox analysis with patient-level clustering and in-field failure coding would settle whether size and immunosuppression hold up, and a prospective dose comparison restricted to lesions of 2 cm or more would answer the question this cohort cannot.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Dose did not predict control (EQD2 OR 1.007, p=0.4735), while size ≥2 cm (OR 2.090) and immunosuppression (OR 2.939) did. Within the 40/10 and 50/20 schedules used here, escalation is not supported; the photon OR marks deeper, larger targets rather than inferior technique.

open_questions: Does dose escalation improve control for NMSC ≥2 cm?
Optimal RT approach for immunosuppressed pts with cutaneous SCC
Late recurrence rates beyond 2 years after skin RT

studies.name: Volume threshold of brain metastases for Linac-based SRS
studies.tldr: In a GK-vs-VMAT replanning study, GK beat VMAT on plan quality for targets ≤0.4 cc, while VMAT won for targets >0.4 cc.
details: 🔍 Retrospective planning study at one institution: 26 pts, 2-3 brain mets each, 76 lesions total
🔍 Pts were drawn from 121 GK pts treated 2018-2019; each was replanned with SmartArc (Pinnacle) and HyperArc (Eclipse)
🔍 Linac delivery used HD-120 MLC and FFF beams; median 3 targets per pt
🔍 Metrics: RTOG CI, Paddick GI, NT V12Gy, V4.5Gy. ROC analysis on CI and NT V12Gy set the threshold volumes

details.text: 📊 Median plan metrics split at the proposed 0.4 cc threshold (Table 4)

details: 📊 For >0.4 cc, NT V12Gy favored VMAT: GK 3.87 vs SmartArc 3.04, and GK 4.06 vs HyperArc 3.57 (both p<0.0001)
📊 Median beam-on time: GK 56.25 min, SmartArc 8.33 min, HyperArc 13.58 min (p<0.0001 vs GK)
⚠️ The 0.4 cc cutoff is an average of four ROC thresholds (0.4, 0.2, 0.4, 0.5 cc), not a prespecified or validated threshold
⚠️ Text calls HyperArc CI 'comparable' to GK for ≤0.4 cc, but Table 4 shows 1.46 vs 1.68, p=0.032
⚠️ Dosimetric surrogates only; no local control, radionecrosis, or clinical outcome data
⚠️ Some adjacent targets were excluded (71 of 76 for CI, 60 for V12Gy) because their isodose volumes could not be separated
🔗 Potrebko et al used a 1.16 cc mean-volume split. Vergalasova et al found VMAT CI better than GK above 1 cm diameter. Bins differ, so direct comparison is limited

verdict.rationale: Single-institution retrospective replanning with dosimetric surrogates only. The threshold is an unvalidated average of ROC cutoffs, with no clinical toxicity or control endpoint.
verdict.audience: 2-3 brain metastases, SRS candidates, GK vs linac VMAT planning

studies.significance: HyperArc shrinks the GK advantage on small targets: for lesions ≤0.4 cc, NT V12Gy was 0.79 vs GK 0.70 (p=0.1923), while SmartArc was clearly worse at 1.25 (p=0.0019). The cutoff depends on the platform, and VMAT beam-on time was 8.33 to 13.58 min vs GK's 56.25.
studies.monday_clinic: For a pt with 2-3 brain mets where every target is >0.4 cc, this supports VMAT-based linac SRS as dosimetrically equal or better than GK with shorter beam-on time. It does not settle platform choice for sub-0.4 cc lesions or for >3 targets.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Retrospective treatment-planning comparison at one institution. **26 pts, 76 lesions**, each GK plan replanned with SmartArc and HyperArc. ROC analysis on RTOG CI and NT V12Gy set the threshold volumes.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Pts treated with GK SRS for brain metastases in 2018-2019 who had **two or three targets** (26 selected from 121). Targets with a prescription below 12 Gy were excluded from the V12Gy analysis.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Linac plans used **HD-120 MLC with FFF beams**, with one or two isocenters per pt. Example prescriptions ranged from 13 Gy to 24 Gy single fraction.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: The ROC thresholds were **0.4 cc** for SmartArc (CI and V12Gy), **0.2 cc** for HyperArc CI and **0.5 cc** for HyperArc V12Gy. Averaged, they give the proposed **0.4 cc** cutoff: GK is favored at or below it and VMAT above it. Median beam-on time was 56.25 min for GK vs 8.33 and 13.58 min for VMAT.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: This is consistent with Liu et al, where VMAT matched or beat GK at a median volume of 0.5 cc. Potrebko et al and Vergalasova et al split targets by mean volume or diameter bins and planned more targets per pt (median eight and seven), so their cutoffs are not directly comparable.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents SRS planning for 2-3 brain mets on an HD-120 MLC FFF linac. Does not represent >4 lesions, 5 mm MLC platforms, or clinical outcomes.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The cutoff is an **average of four ROC thresholds**, not tested in a validation set. For ≤0.4 cc, Table 4 shows HyperArc CI 1.46 vs GK 1.68 (p=0.032), which conflicts with the text's 'comparable conformity'. Closely adjacent targets were dropped, and these are exactly the cases where MLC dose bridging matters most.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The useful signal is that the threshold depends on the platform: HyperArc stays competitive with GK on small-target V12Gy where SmartArc does not. **No clinical endpoint** links these dosimetric differences to radionecrosis or local control.

studies.interpretation:
The question this paper asks is practical: as linac VMAT radiosurgery displaces dedicated Gamma Knife units in many departments, which lesions still justify the GK workflow? The answer offered, a 0.4 cc cutoff, is clean and easy to remember. It deserves less confidence than its precision suggests. The number is not a single ROC-optimal point. It is the average of four thresholds (0.4, 0.2, 0.4 and 0.5 cc) from two planning systems and two metrics, and it was never tested on a held-out set. The individual thresholds are the more honest result, and they say the crossover depends on the platform. With HyperArc, conformity crossed over at 0.2 cc, and small-target NT V12Gy was not significantly different from GK (0.79 vs 0.70, p=0.1923). With SmartArc, GK was clearly better on every metric below the cutoff.

That distinction matters more than the headline. A department running a modern single-isocenter multi-target solution should read this as evidence that the small-lesion gap is narrow and mostly confined to low-dose spread (V4.5Gy and GI). A department running a generic VMAT optimizer should read it as a reason to keep sub-0.4 cc lesions on a sharper-penumbra system when one is available. There is also a reporting inconsistency to note. Table 4 shows HyperArc RTOG CI 1.46 vs GK 1.68 (p=0.032) for small targets, which reads as HyperArc being more conformal, yet the text calls conformity comparable. The table may define CI differently or the columns may be transposed, but a reader cannot resolve it from the source.

Against the prior literature the direction is consistent. Liu et al reported VMAT matching or beating GK at a median volume of 0.5 cc. Vergalasova et al found VMAT conformity better than GK above roughly 1 cm diameter. Potrebko et al found a V12Gy advantage for GK in their small-target group. The present cohort had fewer targets per pt (median three, vs eight and seven in those series), and the authors acknowledge that MLC leakage between targets worsens with more lesions. The 0.4 cc cutoff should therefore be read as a best case for VMAT, not something that carries over to 5-10 lesion cases.

The larger gap is clinical. Every endpoint here is dosimetric. NT V12Gy is a reasonable radionecrosis surrogate, but the absolute small-target differences (fractions of a cc) are unlikely to separate pts on toxicity, and none of these plans was delivered. Excluding closely adjacent targets removes exactly the geometry where dose bridging would penalize VMAT most. What would make the conclusion wrong is a validation set in which the crossover shifts substantially, or clinical data showing that sub-cc V12Gy differences of this size do not change necrosis rates. The 56 vs 8 to 14 min beam-on difference is the most robust finding in the paper, and for many pts it will weigh more than a small conformity edge on a tiny lesion.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: HyperArc shrinks the GK advantage on small targets: for lesions ≤0.4 cc, NT V12Gy was 0.79 vs GK 0.70 (p=0.1923), while SmartArc was clearly worse at 1.25 (p=0.0019). The cutoff depends on the platform, and VMAT beam-on time was 8.33 to 13.58 min vs GK's 56.25.

open_questions: Do sub-0.4 cc dosimetric differences translate into radionecrosis or local control differences?
Does the threshold hold with more than three targets per patient?
Is the averaged 0.4 cc cutoff reproducible in an independent validation cohort?

Predictors of Recurrence after Radiotherapy for Non-Melanoma Skin Cancer
papers.abstract: Predictive factors of recurrence were examined in 448 non-melanoma skin cancers (72% basal cell carcinoma, 28% squamous cell carcinoma) treated with radiotherapy. The overall recurrence rate was 15.8% at a median follow-up of 18.4 months. In multivariate analysis, significant factors for recurrence were age (p = 0.0197), tumour size 2 cm or greater (p = 0.0095), immunosuppression (p = 0.0082), and treatment modality (p = 0.0009).
